query: For boride-based components used in hot-dip aluminum-plating equipment, what single intervention could improve resistance to molten-aluminum corrosion? Formulate one hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts the improvement relative to an appropriate baseline, defines the conditions under which it should remain effective, cites supporting prior evidence, and specifies a controlled experiment whose results could falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: A controlled pre-oxidation heat treatment that produces an in situ, dense, alumina‐rich oxide interlayer on the surface of boride-based components will significantly improve their resistance to molten-aluminum corrosion in hot-dip aluminum-plating equipment.
generation.material_initial_state: Boride-based components with a typical, unmodified surface that is susceptible to rapid attack by molten aluminum.
generation.intervention: Subject the components to a brief, controlled pre-oxidation heat treatment in an oxygen-containing atmosphere to induce the formation of a continuous and adherent alumina-rich oxide layer.
generation.conditions: The treatment is performed under conditions mimicking hot-dip aluminum plating (e.g., similar thermal profiles and atmospheric composition) to ensure that the resulting protective layer remains effective during exposure to molten aluminum.
generation.structural_mediator: An in situ formed, dense alumina-rich oxide layer acting as a diffusion barrier between the molten aluminum and the boride substrate.
generation.mechanism: The pre-oxidation treatment promotes the formation of an oxide film that minimizes direct molten aluminum contact with the substrate, thereby reducing elemental dissolution and interfacial reactions that drive corrosion.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to untreated components, pre-oxidized components will exhibit a measurably lower corrosion rate (e.g., reduced mass loss) and extended service life when exposed to molten aluminum.
generation.baseline: Untreated boride-based components in hot-dip aluminum-plating setups typically suffer from rapid molten aluminum penetration and accelerated corrosion due to the absence of a protective barrier.
generation.boundary: The effectiveness of the treatment may be compromised if the oxide layer is not sufficiently uniform or becomes porous/spalls during thermal cycling; optimal treatment parameters (temperature, duration, atmosphere) are critical.
generation.uncertainty: The precise treatment conditions needed to form the optimal oxide layer and the long-term adhesion and stability of this layer under cyclic plating conditions remain to be determined.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two groups of boride-based components: one undergoes the controlled pre-oxidation heat treatment and the other is left untreated. Expose both groups to simulated hot-dip aluminum-plating conditions (with comparable temperatures and aluminum compositions).
measurements: Quantitative mass loss or corrosion rate measurements over set exposure times
Surface and cross-sectional analysis via SEM/EDS to assess oxide layer formation and integrity
Adhesion testing of the oxide layer after thermal cycling
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the pre-oxidized components do not exhibit a statistically significant reduction in corrosion rate or improved oxide layer characteristics (consistent coverage, adhesion, and integrity) compared to the untreated control under identical test conditions, the hypothesis will be falsified.

Thermal Stability and Hot Corrosion Performance of the AlCoCrFeNi2.1 High-Entropy Alloy Coating by Laser Cladding

Abstract: AbstractBoth crack-free AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloy (EHEA) and Y and Hf co-doping AlCoCrFeNi2.1 EHEA (YHf-EHEA) coatings were prepared by laser cladding. The solidification microstructure, thermal stability, and hot corrosion performance of the coatings at 900 °C under 75% Na2SO4 + 25% NaCl molten salts were investigated. The experimental results showed that the structure of the as-deposited coatings consisted of FCC and BCC/B2 phases. After heat treatment, an Al-rich L12 phase was precipitated in the FCC phase of all coatings. The grain sizes of the EHEA and YHf-EHEA coatings after heat treatment at 900 °C for 10 h increased by 27.5% and 15.7%, respectively, compared to the as-deposited coatings. Meanwhile, after hot corrosion, the spallation areas of the YHf-EHEA and EHEA coatings accounted for 14.98% and 5.67% of the total surface area, respectively. Surface Modification of FeCoNiCr Medium-Entropy Alloy (MEA) Using Octadecyltrichlorosilane and Atmospheric-Pressure Plasma Jet

Abstract: AbstractSurface condition and corrosion resistance are major concerns when metallic materials are going to be utilized for applications. In this study, FeCoNiCr medium-entropy alloy (MEA) is first treated with a nitrogen atmospheric-pressure plasma jet (APPJ) and then coated with octadecyltrichlorosilane (OTS) for the surface modification. The hydrophobicity of the FeCoNiCr MEA was effectively improved by OTS-coating treatment, APPJ treatment, or the combination of both treatments (OTS-coated APPJ-treated), which increased the water contact angle from 54.49° of the bare MEA to 70.56°, 93.94°, and 88.42°, respectively. Potentiodynamic polarization and electrochemical impedance spectroscopy tests demonstrate that the APPJ-treated FeCoNiCr MEA exhibits the best anti-corrosion properties.
